22.t: Working with data: oxygen and sickling
q: Describe the effect of oxygen on sickling in HbS HbS blood.
Less oxygen, more sickling: 2% at 13 kPa rising to 85% at 2 kPa, with a steep rise below about 8 kPa.
Working muscle capillaries can fall to 3 kPa; the lungs are at about 13 kPa. Calculate how many times more cells sickle in the muscle.
Explain how a single base substitution makes the cells sickle.
GAG becomes GTG, so glutamic acid is replaced by valine in the beta chain. The non-polar valine makes haemoglobin molecules stick together into long fibres when oxygen is low, distorting the cell.
Compare the carrier with HbS HbS and explain the difference.
Carriers sickle far less (8% against 70% at 3 kPa), because half their haemoglobin is normal and does not form fibres.
Suggest why people with sickle cell anaemia are advised to avoid high altitudes.
Less oxygen in the air means lower blood oxygen, so more cells sickle and can block capillaries, causing pain and damage.
